Strategy: Reactor temperature is fundamentally an energy-accumulation state (analogous to a mass balance but for enthalpy): dT/dt ∝ (heat generated - heat removed)/thermal mass. The dominant cross-boundary flux term available among the MIC-selected variables is the reactor cooling-water loop: xmv_10 (CW flow valve position) sets the coolant flow rate that carries heat OUT of the reactor jacket, and xmeas_21 (CW outlet temperature) reflects the driving ΔT across the coil — a higher outlet temperature means a smaller temperature gradient and therefore less effective heat removal, which should push reactor temperature up (positive sign). I used lag1 on both actuator/measurement terms since the coolant's thermal effect on the reactor bulk temperature has a short transport/thermal-conduction delay, avoiding same-timestep confounding with the temperature controller's instantaneous response. I added a self-damping term on xmeas_9_lag1 (explicitly permitted) to capture the natural relaxation/dissipation of any accumulated temperature deviation, expected negative (higher previous temperature drives a larger corrective decrease, consistent with a first-order thermal system). I deliberately excluded xmeas_22 (separator CW outlet temp, a different unit's cooling loop) and xmeas_37 (product composition, only weakly tied via reaction exothermicity and analyzer-hold artifacts) to keep the formula a clean instance of the accumulation law rather than a bundle of correlated but unjustified terms. If xmv_10's sign comes out positive instead of negative, that would indicate strong controller confounding (valve opens BECAUSE temperature is rising, not causing a future drop within this lag window) and I will pivot to treating xmv_10 as a control-law regressor (Law 6) or search for a longer lag in a future generation.
